paras: The lynching of James Lacy and Robert Rodrick was the hanging of two prisoners by masked men at Rawlins, Wyoming Territory, in the early morning of March 19, 1882. A third prisoner, William Carter, escaped and later shot at a deputy who tried to recapture him. The story ran nationally in two wire versions that disagreed on the date and on the crimes the men were accused of.

Lacy, Rodrick and Carter were held in the Rawlins jail. According to the Rawlins dispatch, they belonged to an organized gang of thieves operating in Colorado, Wyoming and Utah and had taken part in recent safe robberies, and one of them carried money said to have been stolen at Leadville. A Cheyenne dispatch gave a different accusation: that the men had burglarized several houses and planned to rob the bank until a "pal gave them away."

At 4 o'clock in the morning "a party of masked men" took the three prisoners from the jail and moved them to the stock yards one mile east of town. There Lacy and Rodrick were hanged. The wire report said Carter "was allowed to escape," while the Cheyenne Daily Leader said only that he "made his way out" of the jail at the time of the lynching. No report names any of the lynchers, and none mentions an officer at the jail.

A report that Carter had been captured proved mistaken. On Wednesday, March 22, several deputies went after him at a house near Rawlins known as the "Hog ranch"; he hid in the cellar, fired a six-shooter at one officer, grazing his cheek, and escaped on a horse. No report of an inquest, arrests of the lynchers or Carter's recapture appears in the coverage.

The Rawlins dispatch appeared first in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on March 20 under the headline "Two Men Hanged by Masked Men," and over the next week ran in New Haven, Portland, Los Angeles and Tombstone under headlines such as "Taken From Jail and Hanged," "Lynch Law in Wyoming" and "Two Bad Men Lynched." These versions stated the gang accusation as fact, and the Tombstone Epitaph misprinted the dateline as New Mexico.

A second account came from Cheyenne on March 22 as the last line of a "Reign of Terror" story about incendiaries at Laramie City, which predicted a "necktie party" if the arsonists were caught. That version called the lynchers the "vigilants" of Rawlins, and the Helena Weekly Herald headed it "Lynching Matinee at Rawlins." Midwestern weeklies condensed it into crime roundups titled "Tragical Tales" and "The Bloody Budget of Recent Horrors," the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer calling the dead men "alleged burglars." No paper gave the race of the men who were hanged.

The earliest wire, datelined March 19, placed the hanging at 4 a.m. that day, and the New Haven version, dated March 20, said it happened "yesterday." Other reports put it on March 20: a re-dated wire said "this morning" under a March 20 dateline, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said "Monday," and the River Press said "the 20th." The second man's name was printed as Rodrick, Rolrick, Paddock, Raddock, Roddock, Roddeck and Reddick.

reader.title: Lynching of James Lacy and Robert Rodrick
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Masked men took three prisoners from the Rawlins jail and hanged two of them at the stock yards outside town (A2, A4), and later dispatches said 'vigilants' had 'lynched' them (A6, A8).

Two prisoners were taken from jail by 'a party of masked men' and hanged without legal process (A2, A4), described as the work of the town's 'vigilants' acting against men accused of theft and burglary (A6, A8); no paper names the victims' race.

The Rawlins wire report (A2, A4) and the separate Cheyenne March 22 dispatch (A6, A7, A8) agree that two named men were lynched at Rawlins, and the Cheyenne Daily Leader confirms the jailbreak and lynching locally (A14), though they differ on the date and the charges.
